The platter of roasted salmon sat between them, a pale pink island of forced normalcy. Clara smoothed her napkin for the third time.

“The fish is wonderful, Julian,” she said. Her voice was light, effortless.

I’m leaving you on Tuesday, she thought. The tickets are bought. The bags are packed in the trunk of the car you think is just at the shop for a brake job.

Julian smiled, the corners of his eyes crinkling in a way that used to make her chest ache. Now it just felt like a rehearsed gesture.

“You always did like the skin crisp,” he said. He poured more Chardonnay into her glass, the golden liquid catching the candlelight.

I know about the money, he thought. The six thousand gone from the joint savings. The hidden credit card. The little slips of paper you tucked under the coasters. I’ve known for weeks. I just wanted to see if you’d tell me.

“It’s just nice to have a quiet night,” Clara said, taking a sip of the wine. “We’ve both been so stressed lately.”

I can’t sleep in our bed anymore, she thought. The silence there is louder than the fighting ever was. I’m shaking just sitting here, pretending I’m not counting the minutes until I can walk out the door.

Julian nodded slowly, leaning back in his chair. “It’s been a while since we just… sat. I missed this.”

I’m not angry, he thought. I’m just hollow. I keep waiting for you to say you’re sorry, but you’re acting like everything is fine. Like you’re already gone.

“Do you remember our first anniversary?” Clara asked, her smile widening just a fraction. “The little cottage in Maine? With the leaking roof?”

I wish we could go back, she thought. Before I realized I couldn’t breathe in this house. Before the love turned into a duty. I’m sorry I’m stealing your peace, but I have to find mine.

“I remember,” Julian said softly. He reached across the table, his fingers grazing hers.

I’d give you everything back, he thought. The money, the house, the pride. Just tell me the truth. Tell me why you’re lying to me.

Clara didn’t pull her hand away. She let it lie there, still and numb.

“It was a good time,” she said.

I’m sorry, she thought.

“Yeah,” Julian replied. “It really was.”

I’m not letting go, he thought.

They sat in silence for a moment, the only sound the distant hum of the refrigerator and the ticking of the clock in the hallway—marking the time until the table was cleared, and the pretense finally broke.

The silver forks scraped the porcelain in a rhythmic, careful dance. Between them sat a lemon-butter sea bass, smelling of saltwater and effort.

“It’s wonderful, Elias,” Claire said, her voice soft, steady, perfectly pitched for a Tuesday evening. “Really. You didn’t have to go to all this trouble.”

Elias smiled. It was the smile he used for clients, for her mother, for the mirror when he needed to remember who he was pretending to be. He looked at her—the way her hair fell over one shoulder, the small gold ring on her finger.

“I wanted to,” he said. “I felt like we haven’t had a real night in weeks.”

Because you’ve been coming home at midnight, she thought. Because you smell like a city you’ve never lived in and a person I don’t know.

“You’re right,” Claire said. She took a sip of the Sauvignon Blanc, letting it settle before she spoke again. “Life has been… frantic. Between the firm and the renovation, I feel like I’m barely here.”

Because I’m not, she told herself. Because every time I close my eyes, I’m in that apartment in Montreal. With him. And I can still feel the way the humidity clung to the sheets.

“You’ve been working too hard,” Elias said. He reached across the table, his fingers barely brushing hers.

Claire didn’t pull away. She let him hold her hand for a second too long.

“Maybe,” she whispered. “But it’s almost over. The final audit is on Friday.”

“Good. Then we can breathe again.”

I can’t breathe, he thought. I haven’t breathed since February.

He thought of the burner phone in his glove box. He thought of the woman with the sharp jaw and the low voice who called him in the dark, speaking in a language he had spent ten years pretending he forgot. He thought of the money moving between accounts that didn’t exist. He thought of the life he had built for Claire—this beautiful, fragile house of cards—and how it was currently leaning into a wind he couldn’t stop.

“I missed this,” he said aloud. “Just us.”

Claire smiled back. It was a mirror of his own.

“Me too.”

She felt the weight of the earring in her purse—the one she’d bought with the money she’d been skimming from the company for six months. Not for greed. For a flight. For a deposit on a studio he’d mentioned in passing. For a life where she didn’t have to pretend she was enough for a man who looked at her as if she were a prize he’d already won.

“Pass the salt?” she asked.

He handed it to her. His fingers grazed hers again.

“You’re so quiet tonight,” he said softly.

“Just thinking,” she replied.

“About?”

She looked at him. Truly looked at him. He looked tired. He looked like he was grieving something he couldn’t name. For a moment, she wanted to tell him. I’m leaving. I’m not who you think I am.

He looked back. For a moment, he wanted to say, I’m not the man you married. I’m a ghost in my own house.

But instead, he leaned in and kissed her cheek.

“I love you,” he said.

Claire leaned into him, closing her eyes.

“I love you too,” she lied.
